match.reason: The bank point covers alternative sentencing methods (circle sentencing and restorative justice), not the rights of victims to give evidence by video link, be informed of proceedings, or be told of an offender's likely release, so it teaches a different idea.

draft.title: Rights of victims
card: A victim of crime has certain rights in the criminal justice system. These recognise that giving evidence can be stressful.
Evidence
Victims can give evidence in other ways, such as by video link from a separate room, so they do not face the accused in the courtroom.
Information
Victims can be told about the proceedings, such as what charges have been laid and how the case is going.
Release
Victims can be told when the offender is likely to be released from prison.
draft.remember: Victims are supported to take part and are kept informed.

a.q: A witness in a violent assault case gives evidence by video link from another room. What is the main purpose of this?
opts: To reduce the stress of facing the accused in court
To make the trial a summary hearing
To stop the accused from hearing the evidence
To give the victim a say in the sentence
a.why: Video link lets a victim give evidence without being in the same room as the accused, which reduces stress. It does not change the type of hearing.
a.clue: Think about how the victim feels in the courtroom.

b.q: Jess was the victim of a burglary. Years later, she gets a message saying the offender is likely to be released soon. Which right is this?
opts: The right to be told when the offender is likely released
The right to be told about the court proceedings
The right to give evidence by video link
The right to be presumed innocent
b.why: The message is about the offender's likely release from prison, which is its own right. Being told about proceedings is about the case, not release. Presumed innocence is a right of the accused.
b.clue: The message is about what happens after the sentence.

a.best: To reduce the stress of facing the accused in court

b.best: The right to be told when the offender is likely released

problems.detail: The stem calls the person 'a witness', but the options and the card speak of 'the victim'. The question should say the victim gives evidence, so students do not wonder whether the right applies to any witness.
The right option repeats the stem's wording ('likely ... released'), so a student can match words without knowing the idea. It is also ungrammatical: it should read 'likely to be released'.

In Victoria, the Victims Register that gives notice of an offender's likely release is mainly for victims of violent crime. A plain burglary victim like Jess may not be eligible. A violent offence such as an assault would be a safer example.

proposal.title: Rights of victims
card: Victims of crime have rights in the criminal justice system. These recognise that victims have an interest in the case and that giving evidence can be stressful.
Evidence
Victims can give evidence in other ways, such as by video link from a separate room, so they do not face the accused in the courtroom.
Information
Victims can be told about the proceedings, such as what charges have been laid and how the case is going.
Release
Victims of violent crime can join the Victims Register. They can then be told when the offender is likely to be released from prison.

b.q: Jess was assaulted, and the offender was jailed. Years later, a letter from the Victims Register tells her he will soon leave prison. Which right is this?
opts: The right to be told about the offender's likely release
The right to be told about the charges and the case
The right to give evidence from a separate room
The right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty
b.why: The letter is about when the offender will get out of prison, which is the right to be told about likely release. Being told about the charges and the case is about the proceedings, which ended at sentencing. Presumed innocence is a right of the accused, not the victim.
b.clue: The letter is about what happens after the sentence.
